note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: Are amounts integers or decimals?
Should parties with a zero balance be reported?
In what order should parties or transfers be listed?
hints: Each transaction changes exactly two balances by the same amount.
Keep a running balance per party in a hash map.
Sort the party names at the end; every party that appears is reported, even with balance 0.
invariants: sum of all balances is 0
each row is applied exactly once
chooseWhen: Many transactions over a moderate number of parties
tradeoffs: Sorting the parties costs O(p log p); an insertion-ordered output would avoid it but is not deterministic across inputs
hack2hire:677b5ef978175fce2ecdfc12.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: net balance per party

clarifyingQuestions: Are amounts integers or decimals?
Should parties with a zero balance be reported?
In what order should parties or transfers be listed?
Is the minimum number of transfers required, or a specific greedy order?
hints: First compute the net balance of every party.
A transfer always fully settles at least one of the two parties involved, so there are at most p-1 transfers.
Keep creditors and debtors in two heaps ordered by (amount descending, name ascending); push back the party that is left with a remainder.
invariants: sum of open credits equals sum of open debts
each transfer zeroes at least one party
chooseWhen: A deterministic settlement plan is needed and the number of parties is large
tradeoffs: The greedy plan has at most p-1 transfers but is not always the minimum possible; finding the true minimum is NP-hard

constraints: |literal| <= 1e9, so every partial result stays below 2**53
clarifyingQuestions: Can literals be negative?
Can add take more than two arguments?
Can whitespace appear inside the expression?
hints: A call can only be evaluated after all of its arguments are known.
Push a frame when you read a function name and its "("; finish a literal at "," or ")".
On ")" pop the frame, apply add or sub to its collected values and append the result to the parent frame; recursion would overflow on deep nesting.
invariants: each open frame holds the values of its completed arguments
the stack depth equals the current nesting depth
chooseWhen: The expression may be deeply nested, so an explicit stack beats recursive descent
tradeoffs: A recursive-descent parser is shorter but needs depth-proportional call stack

clarifyingQuestions: Do factories interact, or is each choice independent?
Which factories count as neighbours?
What should be returned when no valid choice exists?
hints: With no interaction, each factory can be optimised on its own.
The best choice for a factory is its cheapest option.
Add the minimum of every row.
invariants: the running total is the optimum for the rows seen so far
chooseWhen: Choices are independent
tradeoffs: Nothing to trade: one linear pass is optimal

clarifyingQuestions: Do factories interact, or is each choice independent?
Which factories count as neighbours?
What should be returned when no valid choice exists?
hints: Let best[j] be the cheapest valid total for factories 0..i with factory i on option j.
best[j] = costs[i][j] + the cheapest previous value whose option index is not j.
Only the smallest and second-smallest previous values (with their indices) are ever needed; use an infinity marker for impossible states.
invariants: best and second-best come from different option indices
an impossible state stays at infinity
chooseWhen: Rows are long, so the O(k^2) per-row transition is too slow
tradeoffs: Tracking two minima is O(k) per row but needs care with ties and missing indices
hack2hire:6a1a1112c81f779dc6a23797.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: neighbours in a line pick different option indices

clarifyingQuestions: Do factories interact, or is each choice independent?
Which factories count as neighbours?
What should be returned when no valid choice exists?
hints: Root the tree anywhere; each subtree can be solved once its children are solved.
dp[v][j] = costs[v][j] + sum over children c of min over k != j of dp[c][k].
Each child needs only its best and second-best (value, index); traverse iteratively because the tree may be a long path.
invariants: dp of a node is computed after all of its children
infinite values mark impossible choices
chooseWhen: The network is a tree and option lists are long
tradeoffs: General graphs make this colouring problem NP-hard; the tree structure is what keeps it linear
hack2hire:6a2b14eb97d3b4b32966cb00.variantLabel: Inferred level 3: tree neighbours pick different option indices

constraints: up to 1e4 file records with at most 5 collection ids each
at most 2000 distinct collection ids, up to 3000 calls, 1 <= k <= 100
clarifyingQuestions: Which methods does the class expose besides the constructor?
How is the hierarchy given?
Does a file in a parent and a child collection count once or twice in the hierarchy total?
hints: Direct totals are fixed after the constructor, so their ranking can be computed once.
Store, for every collection, its hierarchy total and its parent.
When a child gets a parent, add the child's hierarchy total to the parent and to every ancestor above it.
invariants: hierarchy total = direct total + sum of the children's hierarchy totals
the parent links form a forest
chooseWhen: Queries are frequent and parent links are added rarely
tradeoffs: Incremental ancestor updates cost O(depth) per link; recomputing on query would cost O(subtree) instead
hack2hire:68fbce5f378ce2f46141f920.variantLabel: Inferred: file collection totals with a parent hierarchy

clarifyingQuestions: Should the function return success or the deleted paths?
In which order does getAllFiles list children?
What happens when the path does not exist?
hints: A directory can only be deleted after it is empty.
So every child subtree must be deleted first: a post-order traversal.
Use an explicit stack of (directory, index of next child) so deep trees do not overflow the call stack.
invariants: a directory is emitted only after all of its descendants
each path is emitted once
chooseWhen: Only primitive single-entry delete is available
tradeoffs: Iterative post-order needs explicit state; recursion is simpler but limited by stack depth

constraints: directory depth up to 90 (JSON nesting stays below 200)
clarifyingQuestions: Which directories count: all, or only those under a size limit?
Is the root included?
Are file names needed for the answer?
hints: A directory total is the sum of its children's totals, where a file's total is its size.
Compute totals bottom-up so each entry is visited once.
Walk with an explicit stack and add a directory total to the answer when it is at most limit.
invariants: a directory total is final once all its children are processed
chooseWhen: Every directory total is needed
tradeoffs: Recomputing each directory separately is O(n * depth); one post-order pass is O(n)
hack2hire:696442bb3b4797da7459a055.variantLabel: Inferred: sum of directory totals under a limit

constraints: no self loops, no duplicate edges, no cycles
clarifyingQuestions: Should the bottlenecks be ordered by id or by time?
Can the edge list contain duplicates?
Is there an unlimited number of parallel builders?
hints: A dependency is built at step 1 + the latest step among its prerequisites.
Kahn's algorithm processed one whole frontier at a time yields exactly these steps.
Report a frontier that contains a single dependency.
invariants: every node in frontier t has all prerequisites in frontiers < t
each node enters exactly one frontier
chooseWhen: Unlimited parallelism with unit tasks
tradeoffs: Level-by-level BFS needs the whole frontier in memory; a DFS longest-path computation would also work

clarifyingQuestions: Are courses named by strings or integers?
What is the middle of a path with an even number of courses?
In what order should several answers be returned?
hints: The chain has one start: a course that never appears as the second element.
Map every prerequisite to its next course.
With m = pairs.length edges there are m+1 courses; the middle is m/2 steps from the start.
invariants: next is a bijection along the chain
chooseWhen: The input is guaranteed to be one chain
tradeoffs: A two-pointer walk would avoid knowing the length but the length is known here
hack2hire:67e4a80550b60b77022f3848.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: middle of a single chain

constraints: acyclic, no self loops, no duplicate pairs
clarifyingQuestions: Are courses named by strings or integers?
What is the middle of a path with an even number of courses?
In what order should several answers be returned?
hints: The number of paths can be exponential, so do not enumerate them.
A course v is the middle of a path with a courses before it and b after it exactly when b == a or b == a + 1.
Propagate sets of possible a values forward and b values backward in topological order; bitsets make the union a shift and an OR.
invariants: up(v) holds exactly the distances of start-to-v paths
down(v) holds exactly the distances of v-to-end paths
chooseWhen: Many overlapping paths share prefixes and suffixes
tradeoffs: Bitsets cost O(n) bits per course; with at most 1000 courses that is small
hack2hire:67e4adbf50b60b77022f384b.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: middle courses of all start-to-end paths

clarifyingQuestions: Is the entrance an exit if it is on the border?
What is returned when no exit is reachable?
Which exit wins when several are equally near?
hints: All moves cost the same, so breadth-first search finds shortest distances.
Mark cells visited when they are enqueued so each is processed once.
The first border cell dequeued that is not the entrance is the answer.
invariants: the queue holds cells in non-decreasing distance order
chooseWhen: Unweighted grid shortest path
tradeoffs: BFS uses O(cells) memory; bidirectional search does not apply because the exit set is large
hack2hire:68f93bebd7ff180d0ab95208.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: moves to the nearest exit

clarifyingQuestions: Is the entrance an exit if it is on the border?
What is returned when no exit is reachable?
Which exit wins when several are equally near?
hints: Breadth-first search reaches cells in order of distance.
Process the queue one distance level at a time.
Finish the whole level where the first exit appears and keep the smallest (row, col) among its exits.
invariants: all cells of one level share the same distance
chooseWhen: Ties among equally near exits must be broken deterministically
tradeoffs: Stopping at the first dequeued exit is wrong here: the whole level must be scanned
hack2hire:68f9a7290fa32e4d82f4fb89.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: coordinates of the nearest exit

constraints: events.length <= 1e5 with at most 500 distinct users
times and counts are decimal strings in 0..1e9, startAt <= endAt
clarifyingQuestions: Do events after processingTime count?
Is a redeem beyond the limit an error or ignored?
Which users appear in the output?
hints: Only the count per (user, offer) matters.
Apply each event to its counter only when it falls inside the offer window and not after processingTime.
At the end list, per user, the offers active at processingTime whose counter is below the limit.
invariants: 0 <= count(user, offer) <= maxCount
chooseWhen: Events arrive unsorted but must be applied in input order
tradeoffs: Output size is users x active offers in the worst case
hack2hire:6a5e8727bd09995a83107ec3.variantLabel: Inferred: per-user redeemable offers after an event replay

clarifyingQuestions: Can two words be equal?
Can a word be a prefix of another?
Must the order of the input be kept?
hints: A prefix is shared with another word only if it is shared with a lexicographic neighbour.
After sorting, compute the common prefix length with the previous and next word.
The answer is the first max(lcp_prev, lcp_next) + 1 characters.
invariants: in sorted order, the longest common prefix with any other word is attained by a neighbour
chooseWhen: A simple alternative to a counting trie
tradeoffs: A trie gives O(S) time but allocates a node per character; sorting is O(S log n) with less memory

clarifyingQuestions: Does "smallest" mean smallest capacity or smallest index?
Are interval endpoints inclusive?
What is returned when no hub fits?
hints: A hub is usable only if it has enough capacity and no conflicting booking.
Two inclusive intervals overlap exactly when each starts no later than the other ends.
Scan the hubs once and keep the eligible one with the smallest (capacity, index).
invariants: the kept hub is the best eligible hub among those scanned
chooseWhen: One task is placed once
tradeoffs: For many tasks against the same hubs, sorted bookings with binary search would pay off
hack2hire:687e85b47bd121d1f502da90.variantLabel: Inferred: smallest available hub with enough capacity

clarifyingQuestions: What makes a pair special?
Are pairs ordered or unordered, and can i == j?
Should the pairs or their count be returned?
hints: The reverse complement of the reverse complement is the original, so the relation is symmetric.
Count pairs with a hash map instead of comparing all pairs.
For each sequence in order, add how many earlier sequences equal its reverse complement, then record the sequence.
invariants: the map holds counts of sequences[0..j-1]
chooseWhen: Many sequences, exact matching
tradeoffs: Hashing every string costs O(S) memory; the quadratic scan needs none

clarifyingQuestions: Is the limit inclusive?
What happens on two signins in a row?
Should users be returned sorted?
hints: Each user only needs the start time of their currently open session.
On signout with an open session, compare the duration with maxTime and close it.
Collect valid users in a set and sort at the end.
invariants: open[u] is the latest signin of u since u's last processed signout
chooseWhen: Logs are already chronological
tradeoffs: Unsorted logs would need sorting first
hack2hire:68acfc391bf7d2097f647f71.variantLabel: Inferred: users with a session no longer than maxTime

clarifyingQuestions: How are ties broken?
What is returned when no city shares a coordinate?
Can two cities share both coordinates?
hints: Only cities on the same vertical or horizontal line matter.
On a line sorted by the other coordinate, the nearest city on each side is the adjacent one.
Compare at most four neighbours (two per line) by (distance, name).
invariants: within a group, sorted order by the free coordinate
distinct points make adjacent entries the nearest on each side
chooseWhen: Many queries over a fixed city set
tradeoffs: Sorting two groupings costs O(n log n) up front; a hash of lines with linear scans is quadratic in the worst case

clarifyingQuestions: Do digit values act as weights?
Is the answer counted in cells or in moves?
What if the start or end is a wall?
hints: Every move has the same cost, so breadth-first search applies.
Use the eight neighbour offsets and skip walls and visited cells.
The distance of the target cell plus one is the number of cells on the path.
